name: MathHelp.com
line: MathHelp.com teaches lesson by lesson, by video. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs MathHelp.com: MathHelp.com teaches by video lesson, then quizzes. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: MathHelp.com teaches in lessons, each built around a teacher's video on one concept, then guided practice, then quizzes and tests, in a course chosen by grade or subject [3][5]. In AMP, the problem is the unit and assessment is continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In MathHelp.com the unit is the lesson. Each one is built around a short video on a single concept from a classroom teacher, followed by guided practice with audio explanations [4][5][9]. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages; the data are correlational [12].

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. In MathHelp.com the family picks a course by grade or subject [3]. The learner works through its chapters of lessons, setting their own pace inside each lesson, with quizzes and tests after lessons [4][5].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. MathHelp.com's courses are chapters of lessons, each on a single concept, with quizzes and tests after them [5]. We found no scheduled return to earlier lessons in its course pages or answers to common questions [5][8]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks. The mixed practice was also spaced [11].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus on one map of skills. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. MathHelp.com has one course for each grade or subject, from 4th grade math through Algebra 2, and the family chooses which one a learner takes [1][3].

rows.range: 4th grade math through Algebra 2, one course per grade or subject. Also college math and test-prep courses [1][2].
rows.start: The family picks a course by grade or subject [3]. A testimonial on the Algebra 1 page mentions a diagnostic quiz; the page does not describe it [5].
rows.teaching: A short video on one concept from a classroom teacher, then guided practice with audio explanations [4][5][9].
rows.next: The course's chapters of lessons. The learner sets the pace inside each lesson [4][5].
rows.review: None found in the pages we read [5][8].
rows.adult: Picks the course [3]. Parents need to give little instruction, the company says [6].
rows.reports: A grade management system, with grade reports to export or print [8].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its site or in Evidence for ESSA [6][10].

theirs: MathHelp.com is a set of online math courses. Mike Maggart, a high school math teacher, founded it with his partner Charlie Hermes, and it began as Algebra 1 lessons on CDs [2]. Its school courses run from 4th grade math through Pre-Algebra, Algebra 1, Geometry and Algebra 2, and it also has college math and test-prep courses [1][2]. This page compares the school courses.

A learner works through a course by chapters of lessons, setting their own pace inside each lesson [4][5]. Each lesson is built around a short video on a single concept, taught by a classroom teacher, then guided practice with audio explanations, then quizzes and tests [4][5][9]. The company calls its courses a "stand-alone curriculum, so no other material is required" [6].
credit: A classroom teacher explains each concept on video, one idea at a time [5][9].
Guided practice comes with audio explanations [4].
Complete courses through Algebra 2, with proofs in Geometry [1][7].

theirs: We found no outcome study of MathHelp.com on its site or in Evidence for ESSA [6][10].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks. The mixed practice was also spaced, so the result combines the two [11]. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages, from correlational data [12]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: Your child learns best from a teacher explaining each idea on video, one course at a time.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
Your learner needs math before 4th grade or after Algebra 2.

questions.question: How is AMP different from MathHelp.com?
questions.answer: MathHelp.com teaches by lesson: a teacher's video on one concept, then guided practice, then quizzes and tests, in a course the family picks [3][5]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does MathHelp.com work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of MathHelp.com on its site or in Evidence for ESSA [6][10].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
